# Adding VIN Search to a Brownfield System

Adding VIN search to an existing application creates a tempting trap: reverse-engineer every
old decision before writing the new specification.  A delta specification gives you a narrower
starting point.  It records the new VIN behavior, identifies the existing behavior that must
remain intact, and gives both repositories a reviewed target for implementation.

## Learning objective

By the end of this chapter, you can propose an additive VIN-search change without reconstructing a
complete specification for the existing applications.  You can also trace the change from the
OpenSpec artifacts through the backend contract, the Angular client, and the verification evidence.

not as an invitation to rewrite the entire system's history.

## Verification checkpoint

A change is generally ready to close when every ADDED requirement works and accepted unit-number
behavior remains unchanged.  The evidence should cover the full 17-character VIN rule, mode
selection, mode-specific validation, the backend contract, and the frontend path.  It should also
include the regression tests for unit-number consumers.

If a test or review finds a contradiction, the change should stay open.  Update the delta or the
implementation at the boundary where the behavior is wrong, then repeat the focused verification.
The new VIN path working by itself would not be enough reason to archive the change.

## What you learned
A brownfield specification can grow one reviewed change at a time.  An additive delta can limit the
new behavior, preserve accepted behavior explicitly, and give the backend and Angular frontend a
shared contract to verify.
